metadata.name: sns
metadata.overview:
Amazon Simple Notification Service is a fully managed messaging service that delivers messages from publishers to subscribers. Publishers send messages to a topic, which acts as a logical access point and communication channel. Subscribers attached to that topic receive each message asynchronously, so producers and consumers stay decoupled.

The service covers two broad delivery patterns. Application-to-application messaging fans a single published message out to many programmatic destinations, including queues, serverless functions, streaming delivery streams, and HTTP or HTTPS webhooks. Application-to-person messaging delivers notifications directly to people through mobile push, text messages, and email.

Amazon SNS is designed to help teams build event-driven architectures without operating messaging infrastructure. Standard topics favor high throughput and broad protocol support, while FIFO topics preserve strict ordering, group messages, and remove duplicates. Subscription filter policies let each subscriber receive only the messages it cares about. Retry policies and dead-letter queues help preserve messages when a destination is temporarily unavailable. Topics support encryption of stored message bodies with managed keys, resource policies for access control, and private network paths from a virtual private cloud.
useCases: Fan a single application event out to multiple independent consumers in parallel — for example, when a customer places an order, one subscribed queue drives fulfillment while another feeds a data warehouse for analysis, without the publisher knowing who consumes the event.

Route operational and security alerts to on-call engineers, sending notifications by email or text message when a monitoring threshold is breached, an auto scaling group changes, or a file lands in a storage bucket.

Deliver transactional and engagement notifications to end users, such as order confirmations, one-time passcodes, and application update prompts sent as mobile push notifications or text messages to devices worldwide.

Decouple microservices in an event-driven architecture by publishing domain events to a topic that triggers serverless functions and queue consumers, letting each subscriber apply a filter policy so it only receives the subset of events it needs.

Preserve and replay message history for recovery and audit — archive published events by streaming them to storage and analytics destinations, or use ordered topics with an in-place archive so a subscriber can replay a chosen time window after a downstream outage.

relationshipToOtherNamespaces.relationship: Core bidirectional integration. Amazon SQS queues are a primary SNS subscription protocol (fanout target), and SQS queues also serve as dead-letter queues for SNS subscriptions. SQS FIFO queues subscribe to SNS FIFO topics; standard queues subscribe to standard topics. The queue resource policy must grant sqs:SendMessage to the SNS service principal, and the DLQ must be in the same account and Region as the subscription.

Lambda functions are a supported SNS subscription protocol; an SNS message invokes the function for event-driven processing. Cross-region delivery to Lambda requires a regionalized SNS service principal in the function policy. Lambda is also the recommended replacement path for message data protection, and is used to drain dead-letter queues.

Amazon Data Firehose delivery streams are a supported SNS subscription protocol used for message archiving and analytics. Firehose subscriptions require a SubscriptionRoleArn IAM role with permission to write to the delivery stream and Amazon SNS listed as a trusted entity.

CloudWatch collects SNS metrics in the AWS/SNS namespace at 1-minute intervals for published, delivered, failed, filtered-out, and DLQ-redriven message counts plus SMS spend and success rate. CloudWatch alarms are also a common SNS event source that publishes alarm state changes to topics.

SNS delivery status logs are written to CloudWatch Logs for Firehose, Amazon SQS, Lambda, HTTPS, and platform application endpoints. The topic's SuccessFeedbackRoleArn and FailureFeedbackRoleArn attributes grant SNS write access to CloudWatch Logs on the customer's behalf.

CloudTrail records SNS control-plane API calls as management events by default (eventSource sns.amazonaws.com), and optionally records Publish/PublishBatch as data events for the AWS::SNS::Topic and AWS::SNS::PlatformEndpoint resource types. CloudTrail is also an SNS event source that can notify a topic when a new log file is written.

AWS KMS provides the symmetric encryption keys used for SNS server-side encryption of message bodies, via the topic KmsMasterKeyId attribute. Publishers require kms:GenerateDataKey* and kms:Decrypt; AWS service event sources publishing to encrypted topics require a customer managed key with a matching key policy statement.

AWS X-Ray provides active tracing for SNS topics, enabled by setting the topic TracingConfig attribute to Active. X-Ray traces requests end-to-end from the topic through Firehose, Lambda, Amazon SQS, and HTTP/S subscriptions. Tracing permissions are configured through resource policies.

CloudFormation provisions SNS resources through the AWS::SNS::Topic, AWS::SNS::Subscription, AWS::SNS::TopicPolicy, and AWS::SNS::TopicInlinePolicy resource types, including encryption, data protection policies, delivery status logging, and active tracing configuration. CloudFormation is also an SNS event source for stack event notifications.

Amazon S3 is both an SNS event source (bucket event notifications published to a topic, using the s3.amazonaws.com service principal in the KMS key policy for encrypted topics) and an indirect destination via Firehose subscriptions. SetSMSAttributes additionally requires granting the SNS service principal s3:ListBucket to deliver daily SMS usage reports.

IAM authenticates and authorizes all SNS API requests using the sns action prefix, and SNS resource-based topic policies use the same JSON policy language. CloudFormation SNS resource types require iam:GetRole and iam:PassRole to attach feedback and subscription roles. SNS supports service roles but not service-linked roles, and ABAC support is partial.

AWS STS supplies temporary security credentials for signing SNS API requests, which the SNS infrastructure security and best-practice guidance recommends over long-term access keys embedded in applications or instances.

Amazon VPC interface endpoints powered by AWS PrivateLink (managed through the EC2/VPC API surface) provide a private connection between a VPC and SNS so messages can be published without traversing the public internet. Amazon EC2 and EC2 Auto Scaling are also common SNS event sources and message consumers.

Amazon EventBridge routes real-time event streams to SNS topics as a target. Note the documented limitation that aws:SourceAccount, aws:SourceArn, and aws:SourceOrgID conditions in a KMS key policy are not supported for EventBridge delivery to encrypted topics.
Amazon EventBridge Scheduler can invoke Amazon SNS on a schedule to publish messages to topics, documented as a dedicated application-to-application messaging integration in the SNS developer guide.

AWS End User Messaging SMS (sms-voice IAM prefix) performs the actual delivery of SNS SMS messages through its global supply network, and owns origination identity configuration, registration, and SMS billing. The AmazonSNSFullAccess and AmazonSNSReadOnlyAccess managed policies embed sms-voice actions scoped by the aws:CalledViaLast condition set to sns.amazonaws.com.

Amazon Redshift tables are a supported Firehose destination for archiving SNS messages, and Amazon Redshift is also an SNS event source using the redshift.amazonaws.com service principal when publishing to encrypted topics.
Amazon OpenSearch Service is a supported Firehose delivery stream destination for SNS message archiving, search, and analytics.
Amazon Athena is used to query SNS messages that have been archived to Amazon S3 through a Firehose delivery stream subscription.

AWS Config records SNS topics as configuration items under the AWS::SNS::Topic resource type, and AWS Config is also an SNS event source that delivers configuration change notifications to a topic (requiring an IAM role rather than a service principal in the KMS key policy for encrypted topics).

Amazon Bedrock Guardrails is the AWS-recommended replacement for the withdrawn SNS message data protection feature, used in a Lambda-based architecture to detect sensitive data in message payloads and log, block, or redact it before republishing.

AWS Security Hub CSPM is documented as a consumer of SNS CloudTrail activity for creating alerts based on unusual SNS actions, supporting detection of unauthorized or unexpected topic and subscription changes.

Amazon Macie is recommended in the SNS security guidance as an advanced managed security service that assists in discovering and securing personal data stored in Amazon S3, complementing SNS data protection controls.

AWS Chatbot (Amazon Q Developer in chat applications) subscribes to SNS topics to deliver native AWS events and custom events into Amazon Chime chat rooms and Slack channels as an application-to-person destination.

Amazon DynamoDB is an SNS event source that publishes notifications such as DAX cluster maintenance events to topics, and requires the dynamodb.amazonaws.com service principal in the KMS key policy when publishing to an encrypted topic.

Amazon Simple Email Service is an SNS event source that publishes email sending events to topics, using the ses.amazonaws.com service principal which must be granted kms:GenerateDataKey* and kms:Decrypt to publish to an encrypted topic.

Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling is an SNS event source that notifies topics of scaling activity. It is one of the event sources that requires an IAM role rather than a service principal to be named in the KMS key policy when publishing to an encrypted topic.

AWS Systems Manager Incident Manager is an SNS event source, and uniquely requires two service principals (ssm-incidents.amazonaws.com and ssm-contacts.amazonaws.com) in the KMS key policy to publish to an encrypted SNS topic.

entities.name: OriginationNumber
entities.overview:
An origination number is a dedicated phone number that identifies your account as the sender of an SMS message. Recipients see this number on their handsets instead of a shared or automatically selected sender. Common types include long codes, 10-digit long codes, toll-free numbers, and short codes.

Origination numbers are leased per AWS Region and are tied to a specific destination country. Amazon SNS surfaces the numbers available to your account together with their country, capabilities, routing type, and current readiness state. You can reference a specific number when publishing a text message so a consistent sender appears to recipients.

Using a dedicated origination number helps recipients recognize your organization and helps carriers distinguish your traffic from unsolicited messages. It also gives recipients a stable address to reply to when they want to stop receiving messages. Requesting, registering, and releasing the number itself is handled in AWS End User Messaging SMS.

entities.name: PhoneNumber
entities.overview:
An Amazon SNS phone number represents a mobile destination that receives text messages sent from your AWS account. Amazon SNS tracks whether each destination has opted out of receiving SMS messages from the account.

Recipients opt out by replying to a message with a standard keyword such as STOP. While a number is opted out, Amazon SNS does not deliver text messages to it, even if that number is still subscribed to a topic. You can check the opt-out state of an individual number, review the destinations currently opted out, and, subject to a frequency limit, opt a number back in to resume sending.

This helps you honor recipient messaging preferences and satisfy regional regulations that require opt-out handling. Text message delivery and the underlying opt-out list are operated by AWS End User Messaging SMS, which offers more granular opt-out list management for advanced use cases.

entities.name: PlatformApplication
entities.overview:
An Amazon SNS platform application registers a mobile app with a third-party push notification service so Amazon SNS can deliver notifications on your behalf. You create one platform application for each app and push provider, such as Apple Push Notification service or Firebase Cloud Messaging. You supply the provider credentials that Amazon SNS uses to authenticate when it connects to that provider.

Each platform application is the container for the device endpoints that belong to it. When a device registers with the push provider, the provider issues a device token. You register that token under the platform application to create an endpoint representing one app installation on one device. Amazon SNS sends notifications to that endpoint directly, or through a topic the endpoint subscribes to. Delivery reuses the credentials held by the parent platform application.

A platform application also carries operational settings. You can route endpoint creation, update, deletion, and permanent delivery failure events to topics you choose. You can attach IAM roles so Amazon SNS writes push delivery status records to CloudWatch Logs. Amazon SNS tracks credential and token health, and disables endpoints or the application when a provider reports them invalid.

entities.name: SmsAttribute
entities.overview:
Amazon SNS SMS attributes are the account-level default settings that govern how text messages are sent from an AWS Region. They let you cap monthly SMS spending, choose whether deliveries are optimized for cost or for reliability, and set the sender identity that recipients see on their device.

The same settings control SMS observability. You can nominate an IAM role that lets Amazon SNS write a per-message delivery record to CloudWatch Logs, and choose what share of successful deliveries is recorded. You can also name an Amazon S3 bucket to receive a daily usage report summarizing each message that was sent, including its destination, delivery status, and cost.

These defaults apply to every SMS message sent from the account in that Region, and individual publish requests can override some of them. Configuring them helps you contain unexpected spend from misbehaving or abused senders, prioritize delivery of time-critical messages such as one-time passcodes, and retain a record of SMS activity for troubleshooting and compliance review.

entities.name: SmsSandboxAccountStatus
entities.overview:
The Amazon SNS SMS sandbox account status reports whether an AWS account is still confined to the SMS sandbox in a particular AWS Region. It is expressed as a simple in-sandbox indicator for the calling account, so applications and operators can tell which SMS sending rules currently apply before attempting a delivery.

New accounts that send SMS through Amazon SNS begin in the sandbox, a restricted testing and development environment designed to reduce the risk of SMS fraud and abuse. While an account is in the sandbox, SMS messages reach only destination phone numbers that have been added and verified, the number of such destinations is capped, and a low default monthly spending limit applies. Reading the status lets you distinguish sandbox behavior from production behavior instead of inferring it from delivery failures.

The status is scoped to a single account and Region, so each Region is assessed separately. It changes only when AWS grants production access after reviewing a support request, which means the value reflects an AWS-approved posture rather than a setting you configure directly. Monitoring it helps you confirm that accounts intended for testing remain restricted, and that accounts moved to production have compensating spend and destination controls in place.

entities.name: SmsSandboxPhoneNumber
entities.overview:
An Amazon SNS SMS sandbox phone number is a record of a destination mobile number that your account has proven it can reach. Accounts that begin sending SMS through Amazon SNS start in a sandbox, a restricted testing environment designed to limit fraud and abuse and to protect your reputation as a sender. While the account remains in the sandbox, SNS delivers SMS only to numbers held in this verified list.

Adding a number sends a one-time password to the handset in a language you choose. Submitting that password moves the record from pending to verified, establishing possession of the number before any test traffic reaches it. The list is scoped to one account in one AWS Region, holds a small number of entries, and enforces a waiting period before an entry can be removed.

Verified destination numbers apply to both SMS delivery paths: publishing directly to a phone number, and subscribing a phone number to a topic. They let you exercise SMS notification flows end to end during development, and become unnecessary once the account is granted production SMS access.

entities.name: Subscription
entities.overview:
An Amazon SNS subscription connects a topic to a single endpoint that should receive the messages published to that topic. Endpoints can be Amazon SQS queues, AWS Lambda functions, or Amazon Data Firehose delivery streams. They can also be HTTP and HTTPS URLs, email addresses, phone numbers, or mobile push devices. Each subscription is owned separately from the topic, so one topic can fan out to many independent consumers.

Before delivery begins, some endpoint types must prove that their owner intended to receive messages. Web endpoints, email addresses, and endpoints in other accounts stay in a pending state until the owner confirms them. Confirmation can also require signed requests for later removal, which helps prevent unwanted cancellation.

A subscription holds the per-consumer delivery settings. A filter policy narrows the messages the endpoint receives, based on message attributes or the message body. Retry behavior, request throttling, and raw payload formatting can be tuned for web and queue endpoints. Undeliverable messages can be diverted to a dead-letter queue for later inspection or reprocessing. For ordered topics with archiving enabled, a subscription can replay stored messages from a chosen point in time.

entities.name: Topic
entities.overview:
An Amazon SNS topic is a named communication channel that decouples message publishers from message subscribers. A publisher sends a message once to the topic. SNS then replicates that message and pushes a copy to every subscribed endpoint.

Subscribers can be other systems, such as Amazon SQS queues, Lambda functions, Amazon Data Firehose delivery streams, and HTTP or HTTPS endpoints. Subscribers can also be people, reached through email, SMS text messages, or mobile push notifications. This lets a single event trigger parallel, asynchronous processing across many independent consumers without the publisher knowing who they are.

Topics come in two forms. Standard topics favour high throughput and support every delivery protocol. FIFO topics preserve strict ordering within a message group, remove duplicate messages, and can retain messages so subscribers replay them later. Each topic carries its own access policy, optional encryption key, delivery retry behaviour, subscriber filter rules, and tags. That per-topic configuration lets you tune security, routing, and reliability separately for each channel in your architecture.

mitigations.statement: Amazon SNS service API calls on a governed VPC network should only be made against trusted resources or AWS service-owned resources

mitigationContext.context: You can call the Amazon SNS API from your VPC through an interface VPC endpoint (powered by AWS PrivateLink). IAM principals in your VPC can use that path to reach Amazon SNS resources outside your organization. Restricting those calls to trusted resources or AWS service-owned resources helps keep access from your networks within your resource perimeter.

mitigations.statement: Amazon SNS service API calls on a governed VPC network should only be made by trusted identities or AWS services

mitigationContext.context: Amazon SNS can be reached from your VPC through an interface VPC endpoint (powered by AWS PrivateLink). Calls over that network path can be made by IAM principals from any account, including identities outside your organization. Restricting calls over that network path to trusted identities helps keep network access within your identity perimeter.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon SNS platform application should be configured to send delivery status logs to CloudWatch Logs

mitigationContext.context: Amazon SNS can record the delivery status of push notifications sent to your platform application's endpoints. Amazon SNS sends these per-message records to CloudWatch Logs as an audit trail of delivery attempts.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon SNS platform application's success feedback role and failure feedback role should be assumed only by Amazon SNS acting on behalf of trusted resources

mitigationContext.context: An Amazon SNS platform application can reference a customer-managed IAM service role that Amazon SNS assumes to write push delivery status logs. Because you create and maintain that role, its trust policy determines who can assume it.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon SNS SMS attribute should be configured to send SMS delivery status logs to CloudWatch Logs

mitigationContext.context: Your account-level SMS settings include a delivery status logging configuration. When you set it, Amazon SNS can write SMS delivery status logs to CloudWatch Logs.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon SNS SMS attribute delivery status IAM service role should be assumed only by Amazon SNS acting on behalf of trusted resources

mitigationContext.context: Your Amazon SNS SMS attribute settings designate an IAM service role through the `$.attributes{key}` request parameter. Amazon SNS assumes that role to write SMS delivery status logs.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon SNS subscription IAM service role should be assumed only by Amazon SNS acting on behalf of trusted resources

mitigationContext.context: An Amazon SNS subscription for an Amazon Data Firehose delivery stream names a customer-managed IAM service role through `$.Attributes{key}` for Amazon SNS to assume. Because you create and modify that role's trust policy, restricting who can assume it helps limit the role's use to its intended delivery purpose.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon SNS subscription should not allow unauthenticated access to its unsubscribe action

mitigationContext.context: Amazon SNS supports an unauthenticated invocation mode in which `Unsubscribe` against a subscription succeeds without AWS credentials. That authentication mode is a property of the subscription, established when the subscription is confirmed.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon SNS subscription should only be configured with a trusted delivery endpoint: an Amazon SQS queue, AWS Lambda function, Amazon Data Firehose delivery stream, mobile push platform endpoint, HTTP/S URL, email address, or SMS phone number

mitigationContext.context: Creating a subscription persists a delivery destination in `$.Endpoint`, which can point at a resource in any account or at an endpoint outside AWS. Restricting the destination at subscribe time helps keep messages published to your topic flowing only to trusted targets.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon SNS subscription should use the HTTPS delivery protocol to require encryption of data in transit

mitigationContext.context: When you subscribe an endpoint, `$.Protocol` sets whether Amazon SNS delivers notifications over cleartext HTTP or encrypted HTTPS. Choosing `https` helps protect message payloads in transit, because Amazon SNS does not fall back to a cleartext connection.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon SNS topic should be configured to send message delivery status logs to CloudWatch Logs

mitigationContext.context: Your topic can send message delivery status logs to CloudWatch Logs, recording the outcome of each message delivery to a subscribed endpoint. You enable this logging per protocol through the topic's own success and failure feedback attributes.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon SNS topic's success feedback role and failure feedback role should be assumed only by Amazon SNS acting on behalf of trusted resources

mitigationContext.context: Your topic can be configured with a customer-managed IAM service role that Amazon SNS assumes to write delivery status logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Because you create and maintain this role, its trust policy determines which identities and AWS services can assume it.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon SNS topic should have encryption at rest enabled

mitigationContext.context: Amazon SNS stores messages using disk encryption by default. Server-side encryption under an AWS KMS key is optional, applies only after you enable it, and does not cover messages published earlier.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon SNS topic should be accessed only from expected networks

mitigationContext.context: You can apply a resource-based policy to your Amazon SNS topic to grant access to the topic. That policy can limit the networks that requests to your topic originate from.

mitigations.statement: IAM principals should be restricted to accessing only trusted Amazon SNS topic resources

mitigationContext.context: Amazon SNS API calls can specify a topic that belongs to an account outside your organization. Restricting the topics your principals can access helps keep data access within trusted accounts.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon SNS topic should be encrypted with an AWS KMS customer managed key

mitigationContext.context: Amazon SNS supports server-side encryption of a topic's message bodies with a customer managed key, set through the `KmsMasterKeyId` topic attribute. A customer managed key gives you lifecycle control, an audit trail of its use, and the ability to make stored messages unavailable.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon SNS topic's access policy should limit permissions to a subset of IAM principals, rather than granting access to all IAM principals

mitigationContext.context: A resource-based policy attached to your Amazon SNS topic controls which principals can publish to the topic and subscribe to it. That policy can specify a wildcard principal, which would extend those permissions to all IAM principals.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon SNS topic should be accessed only by trusted identities or AWS services acting on behalf of trusted resources

mitigationContext.context: An Amazon SNS topic supports a resource-based policy that can grant principals outside your organization permission to perform `sns:Publish` and `sns:Subscribe`. Restricting those grants to principals in your organization helps keep access to your topic within your identity perimeter.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon SNS topic should be accessed by an AWS service principal, such as the Amazon S3 service principal, only when the service principal is acting on behalf of a trusted resource, AWS account, or organization

mitigationContext.context: An Amazon SNS topic has a resource-based policy that can grant the `sns:Publish` action to AWS services acting on your behalf. You can scope those grants so they apply only to requests made on behalf of resources and accounts you trust.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon SNS topic should be governed by a policy that requires all connections to be encrypted in transit

mitigationContext.context: The Amazon SNS API endpoint that serves your topic accepts requests over both HTTP and HTTPS. Your topic does not automatically reject requests that arrive over HTTP.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon SNS topic should be tagged with information that describes the owner and purpose

mitigationContext.context: An Amazon SNS topic is a durable resource you can tag by its ARN, at creation (`$.Tags[*].Key`, `$.Tags[*].Value`) or later through `TagResource`. Recording owner and purpose tags helps you attribute each topic to a team and a workload.

threats.prerequisites: operating from a governed VPC network
threats.threatAction: can use the governed VPC network to make Amazon SNS service API calls

threatContext.context: Amazon SNS is reachable from your VPC through an interface VPC endpoint (powered by AWS PrivateLink). An IAM principal from an account outside your organization can use that network path to call the Amazon SNS API.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions on untrusted Amazon SNS resources
threats.threatAction: can interact with those untrusted resources from a governed VPC network

threatContext.context: An IAM principal with permissions on those resources can call `Publish` or `Subscribe` through an interface VPC endpoint (powered by AWS PrivateLink). The `$.TopicArn` request parameter can name a topic owned by an account outside your organization. That access enables publishing messages from your VPC to that topic, or subscribing an endpoint to the messages it delivers.

threats.prerequisites: that has been granted access to my Amazon SNS platform application's IAM success feedback role and failure feedback role through their trust policies
threats.threatAction: can assume my success feedback role and failure feedback role and act with their permissions

threatContext.context: Your Amazon SNS platform application designates a success feedback role and a failure feedback role for push delivery status logging through `SuccessFeedbackRoleArn` and `FailureFeedbackRoleArn`. The roles' trust policies can allow principals outside your organization to assume the roles and act with their CloudWatch Logs permissions.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to use an Amazon SNS platform application
threats.threatAction: can interact with the platform application without a record of their activities being persisted by delivery status logging to CloudWatch Logs

threatContext.context: Delivery status logging to CloudWatch Logs emits nothing for a platform application until you configure it. Until then, an IAM principal can use the platform application to send messages to mobile endpoints with no delivery status records persisted.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to modify an Amazon SNS platform application
threats.threatAction: can disable delivery status logging to CloudWatch Logs for the platform application

threatContext.context: Delivery status logging for an Amazon SNS platform application is opt-in, turned on by the feedback role ARN entries in the `$.Attributes{key}` map. An IAM principal that can call `SetPlatformApplicationAttributes` can clear those entries, returning the application to a state that emits no push delivery records; setting `SuccessFeedbackSampleRate` to 0 in the same call stops the records of successful deliveries while failure records continue.

threats.prerequisites: that has been granted access to my Amazon SNS SMS attribute's delivery status IAM role through its trust policy
threats.threatAction: can assume my delivery status IAM role and act with its permissions

threatContext.context: Your Amazon SNS SMS attribute designates an IAM service role through the `DeliveryStatusIAMRole` key of `$.attributes{key}`. You author that role's trust policy, so it can authorize principals outside your organization to assume the role and act with its permissions.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to use an Amazon SNS SMS attribute
threats.threatAction: can interact with the SMS attribute without a record of their activities being persisted by SMS delivery status logging to CloudWatch Logs

threatContext.context: The Amazon SNS SMS attribute holds your account-level text messaging preferences for SMS messages sent through `Publish` to a phone number. While delivery status logging is unconfigured, those sends leave no per-message delivery status record in CloudWatch Logs.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to modify an Amazon SNS SMS attribute
threats.threatAction: can disable SMS delivery status logging to CloudWatch Logs and daily SMS usage report delivery to Amazon S3 for the SMS attribute

threatContext.context: An IAM principal with permissions to modify the SMS attribute can clear the stored `DeliveryStatusIAMRole` or `UsageReportS3Bucket` value with a `SetSMSAttributes` call. Amazon SNS can then stop writing SMS delivery status logs to CloudWatch Logs or the daily usage report to Amazon S3.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify my Amazon SNS subscription
threats.threatAction: can configure my subscription to use an untrusted delivery endpoint (an Amazon SQS queue, AWS Lambda function, Amazon Data Firehose delivery stream, mobile push platform endpoint, HTTP/S URL, email address, or SMS phone number) to which Amazon SNS delivers every message published to the topic

threatContext.context: An IAM principal that creates your subscription can direct every message published to the topic to an endpoint outside your organization or outside AWS. An IAM principal that modifies the subscription can broaden the set of messages that endpoint receives.

`Subscribe` allows you to specify an HTTP/HTTPS endpoint, an email address, or an SMS phone number as the value for the `Endpoint` and `Protocol` request parameters. Because the subsequent requests against the endpoints are not governed by IAM, they are not restricted with `aws:ResourceOrgID` implemented in a service control policy.

`Subscribe` allows you to specify a resource, such as an SQS queue and a Lambda function, that does not belong to your organization as the value for the `Endpoint` and `Protocol` request parameters. Because the subsequent calls against the resources are performed by the service principal, they are not restricted with `aws:ResourceOrgID` implemented in a service control policy.

threats.prerequisites: with a method for enumerating public Amazon SNS subscriptions, or prior knowledge of an existing public subscription
threats.threatAction: can access a subscription that has been configured to allow public access

threatContext.context: An Amazon SNS subscription can be configured to allow access by callers without AWS credentials. A threat actor who enumerates or already knows such a subscription may then delete it and interrupt delivery to the legitimate endpoint.

threats.prerequisites: that has been granted access to my Amazon SNS subscription's IAM subscription role through its trust policy
threats.threatAction: can assume my subscription role and act with its permissions

threatContext.context: Your Amazon SNS subscription using the `firehose` protocol names a subscription role in its `SubscriptionRoleArn` attribute. The trust policy you author for that role can allow principals outside your organization to assume the role and act with its permissions.

threats.prerequisites: with network adjacency to the connection path between clients and an Amazon SNS subscription that has not been configured to encrypt data in transit
threats.threatAction: can capture subscription network traffic and read data in transit that has not been encrypted

threatContext.context: Amazon SNS supports cleartext HTTP as a delivery transport to a subscribed endpoint, and those notifications cross the public internet. Delivery to email and SMS endpoints uses SMTP and carrier networks, for which the subscription exposes no transport encryption setting.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify data in an Amazon SNS topic
threats.threatAction: can encrypt the topic's stored message bodies and FIFO message archive with key material outside the AWS account owner's control

threatContext.context: An IAM principal with `sns:CreateTopic` or `sns:SetTopicAttributes` can set the topic's `KmsMasterKeyId` attribute to a KMS key your account does not administer. If that key becomes unavailable, the topic's stored message bodies and FIFO message archive remain encrypted and undecryptable.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify an Amazon SNS topic
threats.threatAction: can configure the topic without required tagging information

threatContext.context: An IAM principal with permissions to create or modify a topic can call `CreateTopic` without supplying tags, because Amazon SNS does not require them. The topic then has no tag recording its owner or purpose for ownership attribution, cost allocation, and compliance inventory.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify an Amazon SNS topic
threats.threatAction: can encrypt the topic with an AWS managed KMS key, limiting your ability to govern the key's policy and lifecycle

threatContext.context: An IAM principal with permission to create or modify your topic can set `KmsMasterKeyId` to the AWS managed key `alias/aws/sns`. You cannot edit that key's policy, change its yearly rotation schedule, or schedule the key for deletion.

threats.prerequisites: with a method for enumerating public Amazon SNS topics, or prior knowledge of an existing public topic
threats.threatAction: can access a topic that has been configured to allow public access

threatContext.context: Your topic's resource-based policy can grant `sns:Subscribe` to a wildcard principal, leaving the topic reachable by principals in accounts outside your organization. A threat actor who learns the topic ARN can then subscribe an endpoint they control and receive the messages you publish.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify an Amazon SNS topic
threats.threatAction: can create or modify the topic to not use encryption at rest

threatContext.context: Amazon SNS durably stores the message bodies published to your topic. An IAM principal with permissions to create or modify the topic can leave those stored payloads without encryption at rest.

threats.prerequisites: with unintended IAM permissions to read messages from an Amazon SNS topic where the service decrypts data under its own service identity

threats.threatAction: can assume my success feedback role and failure feedback role and act with their permissions

threatContext.context: You author the trust policies of the success feedback role and failure feedback role that Amazon SNS assumes to write your topic's delivery status logs. threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to use an Amazon SNS topic
threats.threatAction: can publish messages that fan out to subscribed endpoints without a record of those deliveries being persisted by message delivery status logging to Amazon CloudWatch Logs, while their control-plane actions remain recorded by always-on AWS CloudTrail management events

threatContext.context: When message delivery status logging is not configured on your topic, no delivery records are written to Amazon CloudWatch Logs. An IAM principal with permissions on the topic can publish messages that fan out to subscribed endpoints, leaving no record of those deliveries.

threats.prerequisites: with access to configure an AWS service that has been granted access to an Amazon SNS topic through its resource-based policy
threats.threatAction: may be able to cause that AWS service to interact with the topic using the principal's data or context

threatContext.context: Your topic's resource-based policy can grant an AWS service permission to publish regardless of which account's resources the service acts on behalf of. An untrusted IAM principal who can configure that service may be able to cause it to publish their content to your topic.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to modify an Amazon SNS topic's delivery status logging
threats.threatAction: can disable message delivery status logging to CloudWatch Logs for the topic

threatContext.context: An IAM principal with `sns:SetTopicAttributes` permission on your topic can clear the feedback role ARN attributes that turn on delivery status logging. Clearing them stops new per-protocol delivery outcome records from reaching CloudWatch Logs; setting a protocol's `SuccessFeedbackSampleRate` attribute to 0 stops that protocol's successful delivery records while its failure records continue.

threats.prerequisites: with network adjacency to the connection path between clients and an Amazon SNS topic that has not been configured to encrypt data in transit
threats.threatAction: can capture topic network traffic and read data in transit that has not been encrypted

threatContext.context: A topic can be reached over `HTTP`, and does not automatically reject requests that are not encrypted. A threat actor on the network path between your clients and the topic can capture that traffic and read the data in transit.

implementationContext.context: This implementation guidance recommends applying the `aws:PrincipalTag/dp:exclude:network` condition key in a service control policy (SCP) to restrict `sns:AddPermission` to principals you designate. This condition helps prevent other principals in your organization from adding grants to your topic's resource-based policy that may allow access from unexpected networks.

This service control policy (SCP) restricts which principals can call `sns:AddPermission`. That action adds grants to the resource-based policy on your topic that carries your network conditions. The network perimeter objective is that your resources can be accessed only from expected networks. You express those expected networks with network conditions in the resource-based policy on your topic. Resource control policies do not yet cover Amazon SNS, so that resource-based policy is where those conditions live. A grant added without your network conditions may allow access from unexpected networks. `sns:SetTopicAttributes` (its `Policy` attribute) and `sns:RemovePermission` also change the topic policy and are not governed by this SCP, which governs only the action that adds grants. A principal permitted those actions can still replace or trim the policy, so the network conditions in the topic policy itself remain the control that applies to every caller.

implementationContext.context: This recommendation directs you to review the resource-based policy on each topic for access granted to identities outside your organization. Remediating unintended access helps keep your topics accessible only to trusted identities, or to AWS services acting on behalf of trusted resources.

This implementation governs Amazon SNS API calls against your topic with the `aws:PrincipalOrgID` condition key, while exempting AWS services that access it on your behalf (`aws:PrincipalIsAWSService`) and scoping those service requests with `aws:SourceOrgID`. As a result, identities outside your organization are restricted from accessing your topic.

Confirm that resource-based policies grant access only to trusted identities and to services acting on your behalf.

As a defense-in-depth measure, use the `aws:PrincipalOrgID`, `aws:PrincipalOrgPaths`, or `aws:PrincipalAccount` condition keys to restrict access to trusted identities. These scope access to IAM principals within a particular organization, specific organizational units, or a specific AWS account, respectively. These keys do not contain your organization or account values for requests by AWS service principals, so apply them only when `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService` is `false`.

To restrict service access to your resources, use the `aws:SourceOrgID`, `aws:SourceOrgPaths`, `aws:SourceAccount`, or `aws:SourceArn` condition keys. These scope access performed on behalf of resources within a particular organization, specific organizational units, a specific AWS account, or a particular resource, respectively. Apply them only when `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService` is `true`. Also require that `aws:SourceAccount` is present in the request context, because not every service integration populates these keys.

Choose the condition key that matches the granularity of the restriction you want to enforce.

Before provisioning, this CloudFormation Hook checks `$.PolicyDocument`, your Amazon SNS topic's resource-based policy, for public access and access beyond your reference policy. It flags AWS service grants without source conditions, helping restrict your topic to trusted identities and AWS services acting on behalf of trusted resources.

A hook here helps prevent your developers from specifying a `$.PolicyDocument`, the topic's resource-based policy, that grants permissions to identities outside your organization. You can also require the standard identity perimeter statement in your topic resource-based policies. Covering both `AWS::SNS::TopicPolicy` and `AWS::SNS::TopicInlinePolicy` addresses every CloudFormation path for granting access to your topic.

This implementation recommends using both IAM Access Analyzer basic policy checks and custom policy checks.

Basic policy checks (`ValidatePolicy`) validate your policy against IAM policy grammar and AWS best practices. These checks do not use automated reasoning. They provide actionable recommendations that help you author policies that are functional and conform to security best practices.

Custom policy checks (`CheckNoPublicAccess`, `CheckNoNewAccess`, `CheckAccessNotGranted`) use automated reasoning to provide a higher level of assurance. They provably verify that a policy does not grant public access, grant new access beyond a reference policy you maintain, or grant specified permissions.

The reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` allowlists the principals that may be granted access to the resource. The check fails when the resource-based policy grants access beyond that allowlist. Example reference policies for resource-based policies are available in the IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks samples repository.

implementationContext.context: This implementation monitors `AddPermission`, `CreateTopic`, and `SetTopicAttributes`, recording `$.AWSAccountId[*]` and the `Policy` attribute values those calls set on your topic. Surfacing those grants helps you detect access extended to identities outside your organization and review it against your identity perimeter.

Monitoring these calls surfaces changes to the resource-based policy on your topic. `AddPermission` carries the account IDs being granted access to the topic. `CreateTopic` and `SetTopicAttributes` carry the `Policy` attribute value. implementationContext.context: This implementation guidance recommends applying the `aws:PrincipalTag/dp:exclude:identity` condition key in a service control policy (SCP) to govern `sns:AddPermission` for principals in your organization. This condition helps prevent principals you have not designated from granting identities outside your organization access to your topics through `AddPermission`.

`sns:AddPermission` adds a statement to a topic's access control policy that grants access to the AWS account IDs named in the request. Amazon SNS is not covered by resource control policies (RCPs), so a service control policy (SCP) is the scalable place to govern these grants. Restricting this action to the principals you select helps prevent grants that reach identities outside your organization. `sns:SetTopicAttributes` (its `Policy` attribute) and `sns:RemovePermission` also change the topic policy. They are not governed by this SCP, which governs only the action that adds grants. A principal permitted those actions can still replace or trim the policy. So the identity conditions in the topic policy itself remain the control that applies to every caller, including principals outside your organization.

This implementation restricts Amazon SNS API calls against your topic with the `aws:SecureTransport` condition key. Requests that are not sent over TLS are denied, so publishers and subscribers cannot reach your topic over an unencrypted connection.

This implementation validates at create time that `$.Tags[*].Key` and `$.Tags[*].Value` carry your required owner and purpose tags on a topic. Rejecting templates that omit them helps address the mitigation by keeping ownership and business function attributable for every topic you deploy.

This implementation flags Amazon SNS topics whose recorded tags at `$.tags[*].key` and `$.tags[*].value` omit your required owner and purpose keys. Surfacing those topics helps you attribute ownership and business function to each topic.

This implementation restricts `sns:CreateTopic` and `sns:TagResource` with the `aws:RequestTag/owner`, `aws:RequestTag/purpose`, and `aws:TagKeys` condition keys, and `sns:UntagResource` with `aws:TagKeys`. Requests that omit the required tag keys in `$.Tags[*].Key` or remove them are denied, so a topic carries an owner and a business purpose.

Use `aws:RequestTag/owner` and `aws:RequestTag/purpose` so that a request omitting either one is denied. Use `aws:TagKeys` to require each key in its exact case because the tag-key portion of `aws:RequestTag/tag-key` is not case-sensitive. Also use `aws:TagKeys` on the untag action so that a request removing either key is denied.
